Home/ESP32 technology

Technology, explained

A computer, radio, and control system on one chip.

ESP32 is a family of microcontrollers designed for connected electronic products. It combines programmable processing, digital and analogue interfaces, Wi‑Fi, and Bluetooth in a compact platform that is accessible to learners yet capable enough for serious prototypes.

Why learn with it

Immediate feedback makes abstract ideas visible.

Change a line of C code and an LED changes state, a sensor value appears, a motor responds, or data travels wirelessly. That short feedback loop helps learners connect software instructions to electrical behaviour.

  • One platform, many disciplines: programming, circuits, control, communication, and IoT.
  • Fast iteration: compile, upload, observe, and improve.
  • Expandable: connect displays, sensors, storage, motors, and network services.
  • Industry-relevant thinking: timing, memory, interfaces, power, reliability, and security.
ProcessorESP32-S3 uses two Xtensa LX7 cores, with clock speeds up to 240 MHz.
Wireless2.4 GHz Wi‑Fi and Bluetooth 5 Low Energy.
Memory512 KB internal SRAM, with support for external flash and PSRAM on suitable modules.
InterfacesProgrammable GPIO plus SPI, I²C, I²S, UART, PWM, ADC, USB, SD/MMC, and TWAI.
DevelopmentBegin with Arduino IDE and C/C++; progress to ESP-IDF when deeper control is needed.
Good forSensor nodes, displays, controls, data logging, wireless devices, and automation prototypes.

The embedded stack

Four layers, one working system.

Troubleshooting becomes easier when you know which layer may be failing.

01

Electrical

Voltage, current, resistance, power, grounding, signal levels, and safe wiring.

02

Hardware

Microcontroller, memory, GPIO pins, sensors, displays, drivers, and connectors.

03

Firmware

C/C++ logic, timing, drivers, state machines, tasks, and error handling.

04

Connectivity

Serial buses, Wi‑Fi, Bluetooth LE, network protocols, provisioning, and cloud links.

C programming model

Setup once. Respond continuously.

Arduino’s structure is simple enough for a first program, but it still teaches the essential embedded idea: initialise hardware, then react to events and time.

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  pinMode(BUTTON_PIN, INPUT_PULLUP);
}

void loop() {
  readInputs();
  updateState();
  driveOutputs();
}

What this teaches

  • Initialisation: configure hardware before using it.
  • Inputs and outputs: turn physical signals into useful behaviour.
  • State: remember what happened and decide what comes next.
  • Timing: design responsive systems without unnecessary blocking.
  • Decomposition: use small functions so code can be tested and understood.
